the secretome of Legionella consists of a complex protein mixture which includes proteins involved in pathogenesis, as well as enzymes which may contribute to tissue destruction during infection.

the characterization of the secretome of L. pneumophila and the identification of OMVs as an important secretion compartment.

the extracellular milieu in the alveolar space of infected lungs is a complex mixture of secreted proteins and lipids, which are released from L. pneumophila by different secretion machineries.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
L. pneumophila secretes a wide range of effector molecules in association with OMV formation, and that these OMVs might be a major delivery vehicle for the virulence factors of this pathogen.
OMV-mediated protein secretion is an important mechanism by which L. pneumophila interacts and modulates the host immune response during infection.
OMVs represent a major delivery vehicle of Legionella virulence factors into the host cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the protein composition of OMVs is complex, which suggests a broad spectrum of functions for these structures in L. pneumophila infection.

OMVs are an important component of the extracellular environment of L. pneumophila, and they may contribute to the pathogenesis of the infection by delivering a large and complex set of virulence factors to the host.
OMVs may be a novel target in the development of new therapeutic strategies against Legionnaires' disease.
